newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania plans reforms of its banking system.
newsitem.headline: Romania plans reforms of its banking system.

text.p: Romania's government adopted draft legislation on Sunday to rule on winding up troubled banks and on improving the post-commmunist banking environment.

"A bank can be declared insolvent if it ceases payments on overdue loans for at least 30 days," government spokesman Nicolae Prelipceanu told a news conference after a meeting of Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea's centrist coalition cabinet.
Under the draft legislation, courts can also rule to wind up banks whose liabilities exceed their assets, Prelipceanu said, without giving details.
The government also approved a planned amendent to a 1991 law which scrapped the comunist-era state banking monopoly.
Romania has some 40 commercial banks, of which 10 are branches of foreign banks.
The government plans to make international audits compulsory.
Foreign banks will have to have branches in Romania before they will be allowed direct financial operations on the local market.
The government is expected to submit the draft laws to parliament, dominated by centrists, in an attempt to keep the reform pledges it made to international creditors in exchange for new loans.
Foreign investors have often cited flawed or ambiguous rules on the operation of banks in Romania as reasons for their reluctance to deal with the Balkan country.
Romania, the former East bloc's second-largest market after Poland, has so far attracted only one-tenth of the capital injected into neighbouring Hungary.
The country's new centrist leaders, who ousted leftists in elections last year, will meet World Bank President James Wolfensohn on Monday to discuss their performance on pledged reforms.
The bank said on Thursday it had agreed to extend some $300 million in loans to Romania ahead of Wolfensohn's three-day visit.
The credits are subject to approval by a bank board meeting next month.
